key_terms.meaning: Energy that travels through space as oscillating electric and magnetic fields, carrying information from a target to a sensor
Distance between two consecutive crests of the wave, measured in metres or micrometres (1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m)
Number of wave cycles passing a point per second, in hertz; ν = c ÷ λ, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light
Energy of one quantum of radiation, Q = hν = hc ÷ λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; shorter wavelength means more energy
A wavelength band where the atmosphere absorbs very little, so a sensor placed there can see the ground
Scattering by gas molecules much smaller than λ, varying as 1 ÷ λ⁴; it makes the clear sky blue
Ratio of reflected radiant flux to incident flux at a surface, a pure number from 0 to 1, often written as a percentage
Radiant flux leaving a unit area into a unit solid angle, in W·m⁻²·sr⁻¹; what the sensor actually measures
The curve of reflectance against wavelength for a surface; its shape identifies the material
The steep rise in vegetation reflectance between about 0.68 μm and 0.75 μm, caused by leaf cell structure
Normalised Difference Vegetation Index = (ρ_NIR − ρ_red) ÷ (ρ_NIR + ρ_red), using near-infrared and red reflectance; values run −1 to +1
A near-polar orbit at about 700–900 km whose plane keeps a fixed angle to the sun, so each pass crosses at the same local time
Sensor with a linear array of detectors that images a whole line of ground at once as the platform moves forward
Sensor that supplies its own energy and records the return, e.g. radar or LiDAR; it works day or night
Ground distance covered by one pixel, in metres; smaller value means finer detail
Number of discrete brightness levels a sensor can record, e.g. 8 bits gives 2⁸ = 256 levels
Time between two images of the same ground point, also called the repeat cycle; measured in days
Relative brightness or darkness of a feature on an image; the most basic interpretation clue
Reading a feature from its neighbours, e.g. a small white rectangle beside a road is probably a building
Image built by putting near-infrared in red, red in green and green in blue; healthy vegetation appears bright red
Assigning pixels to classes after training the computer on sample areas of known class chosen by the analyst

takeaways: Every remote sensing measurement begins with electromagnetic energy, and wavelength alone fixes both the frequency and the photon energy.
Between the sun and the sensor the atmosphere scatters and absorbs energy, so the sensor records radiance that has been altered twice.
The atmosphere is transparent only in certain windows, which is why sensors are built for specific wavelength bands.
Reflectance is a property of the surface; radiance is what reaches the sensor, and the two differ by atmospheric effects and illumination geometry.
Vegetation, soil and water each have a distinct reflectance-versus-wavelength curve, and the differences between the curves allow identification.
A remote sensing system is a platform plus a sensor; orbit choice fixes repeat time and viewing geometry, and sensor geometry fixes image shape.
The four resolutions limit what an image can show, and improving one usually costs another.
Visual interpretation combines tone, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow and association with site knowledge before any software is used.
Digital processing turns raw digital numbers into corrected, enhanced images and then into labelled classes, with an accuracy table to judge the labels.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to run in one line from electromagnetic radiation and its interaction with the atmosphere and target, through sensors, platforms and the four resolutions, to visual interpretation and digital classification, using spectral signature curves as the connecting thread.

bank.q: Explain the wave and particle models of electromagnetic radiation. Show how wavelength fixes frequency and photon energy, and name the spectral regions used in optical remote sensing with their approximate wavelength ranges.
outline: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles, travelling at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
ν = c ÷ λ and Q = hν = hc ÷ λ, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s
Inverse relation: longer wavelength means lower frequency and lower photon energy
Regions: visible 0.4–0.7 μm, near-infrared 0.7–1.3 μm, shortwave infrared 1.3–3 μm, thermal infrared 8–14 μm, microwave 1 mm–1 m
Wave model explains reflection, refraction, diffraction; particle model explains absorption and emission
Why band choice follows the physics: thermal bands detect emission, microwave penetrates cloud

bank.q: Describe how the atmosphere modifies incoming and outgoing electromagnetic radiation. Explain Rayleigh, Mie and non-selective scattering, absorption, and the idea of atmospheric windows.
outline: Scattering and absorption act on the downward solar path and again on the upward path to the sensor
Rayleigh: particles much smaller than λ, intensity varies as 1 ÷ λ⁴, strong in blue, causes haze
Mie: particles about the size of λ (dust, smoke, aerosols), affects longer wavelengths
Non-selective: particles much larger than λ (water droplets, cloud), scatters all visible wavelengths equally, gives white cloud
Absorption by ozone, carbon dioxide and water vapour in specific bands
Atmospheric windows: visible, 1.5–1.8 μm, 2.0–2.4 μm, 8–14 μm, and microwave
Effect on image: reduced contrast, bluish haze, need for atmospheric correction

bank.q: Draw and explain the spectral reflectance curves of healthy vegetation, dry soil and clear water over the visible to shortwave infrared range. State how the curves are used to identify these surfaces.
outline: Vegetation: chlorophyll absorption in blue and red, small green peak near 0.55 μm, red edge at 0.68–0.75 μm, high near-infrared plateau from leaf cell structure, water absorption dips near 1.4 and 1.9 μm
Soil: smooth, gradually rising curve, no sharp features; brightness depends on moisture, organic matter, iron, texture
Water: low reflectance in visible, falls further into near-infrared; turbid water rises in visible; clear water almost black in near-infrared
Snow: very high reflectance in visible, drops in shortwave infrared
Curve shape as a signature; band ratios separate the surfaces
Physical reasons behind each feature, not just shape

bank.q: Classify remote sensing platforms and sensors. Explain passive and active sensors, geostationary and sun-synchronous orbits, and the difference between whiskbroom and pushbroom scanning.
outline: Platforms: ground-based, airborne (aircraft, UAV), spaceborne (satellite, space station)
Passive sensors use reflected or emitted natural radiation; active sensors carry their own transmitter, e.g. radar, LiDAR
Geostationary orbit: about 36,000 km above the equator, same period as the Earth, fixed view, coarse resolution, continuous monitoring
Sun-synchronous near-polar orbit at about 700–900 km, fixed local solar time, global coverage, repeat cycle of days
Whiskbroom: single detector with a rotating mirror scans across track, dwell time limits radiometric precision
Pushbroom: linear detector array images a full line, longer dwell time, no moving mirror, geometric distortions differ
Examples of sensor types: panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral, thermal, SAR, LiDAR

bank.q: Explain the four resolutions of a remote sensing image with suitable examples, and describe the trade-offs between them.
outline: Spatial resolution: ground size of one pixel, in metres; 5.8 m on one well-known Indian imaging satellite versus 10 m to 30 m on open missions
Spectral resolution: number, width and placement of bands; panchromatic single wide band versus hyperspectral with hundreds of narrow bands
Radiometric resolution: bits per pixel, 8 bits gives 256 levels, 11 bits gives 2048 levels
Temporal resolution: repeat cycle in days; geostationary gives minutes, polar orbiting gives days, some high-resolution sensors can be tasked
Trade-offs: finer spatial resolution usually means narrower swath and longer repeat; more bands mean lower signal per band
Application-driven choice

bank.q: A vegetation index image is to be prepared from a sensor whose red band is 0.63–0.69 μm and near-infrared band is 0.76–0.90 μm. Compute NDVI at two pixels: pixel A with red reflectance 0.05 and near-infrared reflectance 0.45; pixel B with red 0.20 and near-infrared 0.30. Interpret both values and state two limitations of NDVI.
outline: Formula: NDVI = (ρ_NIR − ρ_red) ÷ (ρ_NIR + ρ_red)
Pixel A: (0.45 − 0.05) ÷ (0.45 + 0.05) = 0.40 ÷ 0.50 = 0.80, dense healthy vegetation
Pixel B: (0.30 − 0.20) ÷ (0.30 + 0.20) = 0.10 ÷ 0.50 = 0.20, sparse or stressed cover, or mixed soil
Range check −1 to +1; water and cloud give negative or near-zero values
Limitations: saturates over dense canopy, affected by soil background and atmosphere, needs red and near-infrared bands
Why the ratio reduces illumination differences

bank.q: An image of 8000 columns by 8000 rows is recorded at 11-bit radiometric resolution in four bands. Calculate the number of grey levels, the raw storage in megabytes, and the ground area covered if the pixel size is 5.8 m. Comment on how storage changes if the data are stored as 8-bit.
outline: 11 bits gives 2¹¹ = 2048 grey levels
Total pixels = 8000 × 8000 = 6.4 × 10⁷
Bits = 6.4 × 10⁷ × 11 × 4 = 2.816 × 10⁹ bits, divide by 8 for bytes and by 10⁶ for megabytes ≈ 352 MB
At 8 bits: 6.4 × 10⁷ × 1 × 4 bytes = 2.56 × 10⁸ bytes ≈ 256 MB
Ground area = 6.4 × 10⁷ × (5.8)² m² ≈ 2.15 × 10⁹ m² ≈ 2153 km²
Comment: fewer bits save space but quantise brightness and may lose detail in dark targets

bank.q: You must monitor paddy crop growth every week over a district of about 5000 km². Choose the platform type, orbit, band set and resolution, and justify each choice. Then state how you would convert the images into a crop-area map.
outline: Platform: spaceborne, since the area is large and weekly coverage is needed
Orbit: sun-synchronous polar, fixed local time for comparable illumination; swath wide enough to cover the district in one or two passes
Bands: red and near-infrared for NDVI, plus shortwave infrared for moisture; possibly green for visual composites
Spatial resolution: 10 m to 30 m adequate for field-level crop mapping; finer resolution increases data volume without need
Temporal resolution: repeat cycle of about 5 days or better, or a constellation, to get cloud-free weekly observations
Processing: geometric and atmospheric correction, NDVI time series, supervised classification on training fields, accuracy check on ground truth
Mention cloud cover as the main operational risk in the monsoon

bank.q: A raw image has digital numbers between 40 and 120 in an 8-bit file. Explain how a linear contrast stretch, a histogram equalisation and a band ratio would each change the image, and state which you would use to bring out a faint drainage pattern and why.
outline: Raw data occupy a narrow part of the 0–255 range, so the image looks flat and dark
Linear stretch maps input minimum and maximum to 0 and 255, output = (DN − min) × 255 ÷ (max − min); preserves relative brightness
Histogram equalisation redistributes values so each grey level is equally frequent; boosts local contrast but changes relative brightness
Band ratio divides one band by another, cancelling illumination differences and highlighting absorption features
For faint drainage: contrast stretch first, since the pattern is a tonal and textural feature and relative brightness matters; histogram equalisation may amplify noise
Principal component analysis and edge enhancement as further options

bank.q: A sensor at altitude records radiance, but the analyst wants surface reflectance. Analyse the factors that separate the two, and evaluate how atmospheric correction and ground reference data improve the estimate.
outline: Radiance is at-sensor flux per unit area per unit solid angle; reflectance is a surface property
Path radiance from scattering adds a constant bias; absorption removes signal in some bands
Illumination geometry: solar zenith and azimuth angle, topographic slope and aspect change the incident flux
Adjacency effect and mixed pixels from finite sensor footprint
Correction methods: dark object subtraction, radiative transfer models, empirical line calibration against bright and dark targets
Residual error remains; indices such as NDVI and band ratios reduce but do not remove it
Evaluate: relative correction is enough for classification, absolute reflectance needed for multi-date quantitative work

bank.q: Compare visual image interpretation with digital classification for mapping land use. Evaluate when a trained interpreter still beats software, and how the two can be combined.
outline: Visual: uses tone, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow, site and association; needs experience and site knowledge; slow over large areas; reproducible only with effort
Digital: uses pixel values and statistics; fast, repeatable, handles many bands; needs training data and ground truth; suffers from mixed pixels and spectral confusion
Visual wins on shape and context reasoning, e.g. separating a road from a canal of the same tone, and on small areas with fine detail
Digital wins on large areas, multi-band and multi-date data, and quantitative indices
Hybrid: digital classification aided by on-screen visual editing, image segmentation into objects then classification
Accuracy assessment by confusion matrix, overall accuracy and kappa coefficient

bank.q: Two images of the same coastal city, five years apart, are to be used to map urban growth. Analyse the requirements on resolution, registration and season, and evaluate the sources of error in the resulting change map.
outline: Requirements: same or similar sensor and bands, similar spatial resolution, images from the same season and near-same time of day to match sun angle and phenology
Accurate geometric registration to within a fraction of a pixel, otherwise edges produce false change
Radiometric normalisation between dates, since sensor gain and atmosphere differ
Methods: image differencing, band ratio, principal component analysis, post-classification comparison
Errors: misregistration, mixed pixels along boundaries, phenology and tide differences, cloud and shadow, classification error propagating into the change map
Evaluate: post-classification comparison gives a clear change matrix but doubles the classification error; differencing is more sensitive but harder to label
Validate with high-resolution imagery or field check

bank.q: A newly designed satellite must serve both agriculture monitoring and urban mapping. Evaluate how the choice of orbit, swath, band set and spatial resolution constrains each other, and propose a reasonable design with justification.
outline: Sun-synchronous polar orbit gives a fixed local time, useful for both applications, with a repeat cycle of a few days
Narrow swath gives fine pixels but long revisit; wide swath gives frequent coverage but coarse pixels
Agriculture needs red and near-infrared for vegetation indices and frequent revisit, moderate resolution is acceptable
Urban mapping needs fine spatial resolution and panchromatic sharpening, but that pushes data volume and cost up
Design compromise: multispectral at moderate resolution plus a panchromatic band, off-nadir tasking for rapid revisit
Signal-to-noise falls as pixels shrink; radiometric resolution must be adequate
Conclusion: state the trade-off explicitly and defend the chosen numbers

glossary.def: Transfer of radiation energy into a medium, such as a gas molecule or a leaf, so that it is not returned to the sensor.
Fraction of incident solar radiation reflected by a surface over all wavelengths, a single broadband number.
A wavelength interval where absorption is weak, allowing the sensor to see the ground.
A narrow wavelength interval recorded as one image channel by a sensor.
Point operation that maps a narrow range of digital numbers onto the full display range to improve visibility.
Integer value stored for each pixel, proportional to radiance after sensor calibration scaling.
Radiation given out by a body because of its temperature, described by Planck's law.
Image made by assigning three different wavelength bands to red, green and blue display channels; colours are not natural.
Circular equatorial orbit at about 36,000 km altitude where the satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation and appears fixed.
Angular cone seen by one detector at one instant; its projection on the ground sets the pixel size.
Measure of classification agreement after removing the agreement expected by chance alone.
Active system that sends laser pulses and times the return to measure distance and build a three-dimensional surface model.
The point on the ground directly below the sensor; the viewing direction straight down.
One picture element, the smallest cell of a raster image, holding a single digital number per band.
Radiant flux per unit projected area per unit solid angle reaching the sensor, in W·m⁻²·sr⁻¹.
Dimensionless ratio of reflected to incident flux at a surface, ranging from 0 to 1.
Synthetic Aperture Radar, an active microwave sensor that uses platform motion to build a fine-resolution image and sees through cloud.
Ratio of image distance to corresponding ground distance, e.g. 1:25,000.
Redirection of radiation by particles or molecules without absorption, producing haze and path radiance.
Ground width covered by the sensor in one sweep or one pass.
Frequency of tonal change in a group of pixels, giving a rough or smooth appearance used in visual interpretation.
Fraction of incident radiation that passes through a medium, the complement of absorption and scattering losses.
Grouping pixels into statistically similar clusters without training samples, after which the analyst names the clusters.
Sensor that sweeps a single detector across the track using a rotating mirror while the platform moves forward.
